newsitem.title: USA: Clinton expects to nominate Tenet as CIA head.
newsitem.headline: Clinton expects to nominate Tenet as CIA head.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, hoping to avoid another clash with the Senate, expects to nominate intelligence veteran George Tenet as director of the CIA, senior administration officials said on Tuesday.

Clinton, who denounced the cycle of "political destruction" that forced Anthony Lake to ask that he be withdrawn from consideration to run the CIA, has asked for a routine background check on Tenet, officials said.
"As soon as the check is over, it should be final," one official said of Tenet, who once served as the Senate Intelligence Committee's staff chief.

Tenet, 44, has been serving as acting director since John Deutch stepped down in December. He already has been confirmed by the Senate as the agency's deputy director -- reducing the chances the Republican-controlled Senate will reject him.
"The president would like to get this out of the way before leaving for Helskini" on Wednesday night and a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, a senior administration official said.
Tenet drew quick praise from Senate Republican leader Trent Lott, who said: "Barring something I don't know about, it looks like he would be a good choice."

Clinton, calling a small group of reporters to the Red Room of the White House, said he planned to move quickly to name a replacement but complained about the mental gauntlet presidential nominees faced.

"For too long we have allowed ordinary political processes and honest disagreements among honourable people to descend into political sniping, then into political revenge, and too often that results in political destruction," said Clinton, resting his injured leg on a footstool.

He said he had been prepared to fight for Lake, his former national security adviser, for as long as it took to win him Senate confirmation, but Lake was concerned about the effect of a protracted confirmation fight on the CIA.

"I think he was afraid the longer this went on ... the more it would damage the agency," said the president, who is recovering from knee surgery and sat in a chair with his right foot on a stool. He summoned reporters to hear his personal statement on a nomination withdrawal that stunned Washington.

Lake said he feared the agency and his own integrity would be damaged by a prolonged pounding from Republican senators on issues ranging from his knowledge of questionable White House fund-raising practices to his failure to divest himself of some stock and U.S. policy in Bosnia.
Sen. Richard Shelby, chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and Lake's leading antagonist, insisted he "ran a fair hearing," and added, "I was never out to get Mr. Lake."
He said his tough scrutiny was driven by a desire to confirm the "proper person for this very important job."
But the Democratic vice-chairman of the committee, Sen. Robert Kerrey of Nebraska, disagreed, saying "I do not believe the ... process that Tony Lake went through was fair."
